parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian пру́жити (prúžyty). Doublet of prężyć (“to flex, tighten”), an inherited form.
Borrowed from Ukrainian прину́ка (prynúka, “compulsion”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian при́сі́д (prýsíd).
From przemowa + -ka. Sense 3 is a semantic loan from Ukrainian примівка (prymivka).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: space (area as a whole along with the objects within)
parole.testo: Uncertain. First attested in 1562–1566. * From Proto-Slavic *persterti + Proto-Slavic *-nь. * Derived from Ukrainian про́сторінь (próstorinʹ). * Back-formation from przestrzeństwo.

parole.significato: plate, tile (sheet of ceramic or fired clay to cover surfaces)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian пли́та́ (plýtá), from Old East Slavic плита (plita), from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos). First attested in the 18th century.
Perhaps borrowed from Ukrainian гротище (hrotyšče).
Borrowed from Ukrainian різати (rizaty). Doublet of rzezać, an inherited form.
Borrowed from Ukrainian різу́н (rizún). Doublet of rzezuń.

parole.significato: chaos, ruckus (state of disorder; a confused or amorphous mixture or conglomeration)
parole.testo: Uncertain. According to Bańkowski, a loanword from Ukrainian розгардія́ш (rozhardijáš), itself of Turkic origin. However, the chronology and history of the Ukrainian word, which appears in various phonetic variants, speak against such etymologization.
Borrowed from Ukrainian розгово́р (rozhovór). Doublet of rozgowor.

parole.significato: steed (stallion, especially in the sense of mount)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian рума́к (rumák), from a Turkic language.
Borrowed from Ukrainian сади́ба (sadýba). Doublet of siedziba.
Perhaps borrowed from Ukrainian серда́к (serdák).

parole.significato: sich (fortified administrative and military centre for the Zaporozhian and Danube Cossacks)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian січ (sič).

parole.significato: idyllic life or an environment conducive to an idyllic life
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian селя́нка (seljánka).
Probably borrowed from Ukrainian селя́ва (seljáva) or Belarusian сяля́ва (sjaljáva), itself perhaps from Lithuanian seliavà, saliavà, šalvi̇̀s.
Borrowed from Ukrainian солянка (soljanka).
From dialectal Ukrainian спадь (spadʹ).
Borrowed from Ukrainian степ (step).
Borrowed from Ukrainian суга́к (suhák), from Chagatai سایغاق (saiɣak).
Borrowed from Ukrainian сумни́й (sumnýj). By surface analysis, s- + um + -ny.

parole.significato: Surzhyk (pidgin language or interlanguage combining elements of Russian and Ukrainian)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian су́ржик (súržyk).

Borrowed from Ukrainian шарова́ри (šarováry) or Belarusian шарава́ры (šaraváry), or Russian шарова́ры (šarováry), from Hungarian salavári, from Bulgarian шалвари (šalvari), from Ottoman Turkish شالوار (şalvâr), from Persian شلوار (šalvâr), from Middle Persian [script needed] (šlwʾl /⁠šalwār⁠/), from
Borrowed from Ukrainian шалавіла (šalavila).
Onomatopoeic. A reference to Ukrainian що (ščo, “what”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian шовко́вий (šovkóvyj).
Borrowed from Ukrainian сторч (storč).

parole.significato: sloboda (a kind of settlement in the history of Russia, Belarus and Ukraine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian слобода́ (slobodá). Doublet of swoboda.
Borrowed from Ukrainian та (ta).
Borrowed from Ukrainian табу́н (tabún), from Tatar табун (tabun).
Borrowed from Ukrainian тапча́н (tapčán), from Tatar тапчан (tapçan), from Old Turkic, from Middle Chinese 道場, a calque of Sanskrit बोधिमण्ड (bodhimaṇḍa). Doublet of dojo.

parole.significato: taraban (percussive drum-like folk instrument of Turkish origin, which was once used in Ukraine and, to a lesser extent…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian тараба́н (tarabán). Doublet of baraban. Compare Russian бараба́н (barabán).
Borrowed from Ukrainian тарада́йка (taradájka).

parole.significato: any plant of the genus Acorus, especially sweet flag (Acorus calamus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian тата́рак (tatárak).
Borrowed from Ukrainian талала́йство (talalájstvo).
Borrowed from Ukrainian темля́к (temlják), from a Turkic language, possibly Tatar тәмлик (tämlik).

parole.significato: titushky (violent pro-government vigilante involved in cracking down on popular protest)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian тіту́шка (titúška).

parole.significato: manger filled with fodder placed in the forest
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian тризу́б (tryzúb). Doublet of trójząb (“trident”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian ухиля́нт (uxyljánt). By surface analysis, uchylać się + -ant.
Borrowed from Ukrainian вата́га (vatáha), from a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ōtag (“fireplace, tent, room”). Doublet of wataga (“warlord”).
Borrowed from Ukrainian вере́та (veréta). First attested in the 1683-1693.
Borrowed from Ukrainian верта́ти (vertáty).
Borrowed from Ukrainian верте́п (vertép).

From Ukrainian ві́дділ (víddil, “part, section; a military unit”) + -arz, from Ukrainian Самооборонні кущові відділи (Samooboronni kuščovi viddily) (Self-defense Kushch Units), as the Self-defense Kushch Units was one of the Ukrainian militant groups that took part in mass killings of Polish people
Borrowed from Ukrainian віду́н (vidún). First attested in 1850.
Possibly borrowed from Ukrainian ви́караскатися (výkaraskatysja). By surface analysis, wy- + karaskać.

parole.significato: tarsier (any primate of the family Tarsiidae)
parole.testo: Uncertain. On semantic and, above all, phonetic grounds, some derive it from Ukrainian. Compare Ukrainian ви́рла (výrla), вирла́ч (vyrláč), вирла́тий (vyrlátyj), and вирлоо́кий (vyrloókyj).
Borrowed from Ukrainian забу́дько (zabúdʹko).
Borrowed from Ukrainian закоти́ти (zakotýty). By surface analysis, za- + kocić.

parole.significato: to manage (to succeed at an attempt in spite difficulty)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ukrainian зду́жати (zdúžaty). Piecewise doublet of zdążać.
Borrowed from Ukrainian зозуля (zozulja).
Borrowed from Ukrainian зво́щик (zvóščyk).
Borrowed from Ukrainian лахмі́ття (laxmíttja).
Borrowed from Ukrainian ла́щитися (láščytysja), from Proto-Slavic *laščiti (sę).

Borrowed from Ukrainian гли́пати (hlýpaty), from Proto-Slavic *glip- (“to take a look”), of uncertain ultimate origin, either from Proto-Indo-European *gʰlip- or a substrate word of that form, in either case related to Proto-West Germanic *glippōn (“to slip, flee”).
Borrowed from Belarusian благі́ (blahí) or Ukrainian благи́й (blahýj). Doublet of błogi (“blissful”).
Borrowed from Russian хват (xvat) and/or Ukrainian хват (xvat). Related to chwacić, chwatać, chwytać.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from Slovak kapravý or from Ukrainian капра́вий (kaprávyj), ultimately from dialectal Proto-Slavic *kapra.
Borrowed from Belarusian жы́чка (žýčka) or Ukrainian жічка /жи́чка (žička).
